title: Collective Topological Dark Solitons, Platicons, and Bright-Like Solitons in Normal Dispersion Optical Frequency Combs
authors: Seyed Danial Hashemi, Ankitkumar Maisuriya, Sunil Mittal
abstract: Bright dissipative Kerr solitons generated in anomalous-dispersion microresonators underpin integrated optical frequency combs that have enabled applications including precision metrology, spectroscopy, coherent communications, and optical frequency synthesis. In contrast, Kerr resonators operating in the normal-dispersion regime can support dark solitons and platicons, but even the initiation of frequency comb generation typically requires auxiliary mechanisms, such as avoided mode crossings or pulsed pumping, to satisfy the phase-matching condition for four-wave mixing. Here we show that topological edge states in two-dimensional Kerr resonator lattices intrinsically satisfy this phase-matching condition, enabling the generation of optical frequency combs and novel coherent dissipative structures in the normal-dispersion regime without any auxiliary mechanisms. The resulting frequency combs self-organize into collective dark solitons that exhibit large-scale spatiotemporal synchronization across multiple resonators at the entire lattice edge. By tuning the pump detuning, we demonstrate the continuous evolution of topological dark solitons into topological platicons while preserving collective synchronization. Remarkably, we show that the topological lattice also supports collective bright-like soliton states despite all constituent resonators operating in the normal-dispersion regime. Our results establish topological Kerr resonator arrays as a versatile route for engineering a broad family of coherent dissipative structures, ranging from dark solitons to bright-like soliton states, within a single platform. They also provide a route toward integrated frequency-comb generation in material platforms and wavelength ranges where normal material dispersion has traditionally constrained comb generation in conventional single-resonator systems.
summary: This paper shows that topological edge states in 2D Kerr resonator lattices can generate optical frequency combs and various coherent soliton structures, including dark, platicon, and bright-like states, even when the material operates in the normal-dispersion regime. This circumvents the need for auxiliary mechanisms typically required for comb generation in such materials. The findings establish topological arrays as a highly versatile platform for engineering broadband coherent light sources.
main_problem: The research aims to demonstrate the generation of optical frequency combs and various coherent dissipative structures (dark, platicons, bright-like solitons) in the normal-dispersion regime without needing auxiliary physical mechanisms.
main_result: Topological edge states in 2D Kerr resonator lattices intrinsically satisfy the phase-matching condition for four-wave mixing, enabling comb generation and supporting a versatile range of soliton states in normal dispersion.
method: The analysis uses theoretical modeling based on tight-binding Hamiltonians and the Ikeda map formalism to simulate field evolution in coupled resonator arrays.
model_or_system: The system is a two-dimensional Kerr resonator lattice modeled by a tight-binding Hamiltonian, incorporating topological edge states and operating in the normal-dispersion regime.
key_observables: Collective topological dark solitons, topological platicons, bright-like soliton states, and the associated frequency comb spectrum.
important_parameters: Normal-dispersion regime, 2D lattice structure, pump detuning, and coupling strengths (J).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that topological edge states provide an intrinsic phase-matching mechanism, eliminating the need for external pumping or avoided crossings.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the linear absorption spectrum showing edge state resonances, intensity distributions of dark solitons on the edge, and the evolution of the comb spectrum across different soliton regimes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical system and the problem (comb generation in normal dispersion), details the mechanism (topological edge states satisfying phase-matching), and presents results showing the continuous evolution between different soliton types.
why_interesting: This work bridges concepts from topological physics (edge states) with nonlinear optics (solitons/frequency combs), providing a novel, robust platform for integrated photonics that overcomes limitations imposed by material dispersion.

Schematic of the topological ring resonator lattice, with its absorption spectrum and dispersion. The presence of multiple topological edge- state resonances within each FSR intrinsically satisfies the phase-matching condition, enabling frequency comb generation without auxiliary mechanisms...

FIG. 2. Topological dark solitons. a. Linear absorption spectrum of the topological lattice with edge state resonances shaded green. The pumped edge mode is shaded red. The inset shows the nonlinear cavity power. b. Intensity distribution in the lattice showing formation of topological dark solitons in every resonator on the edge. The insets show zoomed-in views at four different resonators. c,d. Temporal output showing dark soliton intensity dips, repeating every τR. e-h. Comb spectrum showing dominant oscillation of a single edge mode at µ = 0, and two side-band edge modes at µ = ±35.

FIG. 3. Topological platicons a. Lattice intensity distribution showing the formation of topological platicons in every edge resonator. The inset shows intensity in the resonator coupled to the input-output waveguide. b,c. Temporal and spectral output. d,e,f. Zoomed in comb spectra at µ = +35, 0, −35, respectively. g. Intensity distribution in the input-output ring showing tunability of the platicon width by red detuning the pump frequency.

Figure 3 shows the formation of a collective topological platicon state, in which each edge resonator supports a syn- chronized platicon characterized by a broad flat-top inten- sity profile with a weak periodic modulation. As in the dark-soliton regime, the switching fronts remain synchronized across all edge resonators, demonstrating large-scale collec- tive synchronization (Fig.3a and Movie M3). The temporal output therefore consists of a periodic sequence of modulated flat-top pulses repeating every round-trip time τR (Fig.3b).
